743.title: The joy of the Lord (Nehemiah 8:1–12)
743.hook: the law is read aloud and people weep; go, eat, share, the joy of the Lord is your strength
743.howItsDone: Some Christians quote Nehemiah 8:10, the joy of the LORD is your strength, in hard seasons, and some churches end a time of confession or lament with a shared meal in the same spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nehemiah's wall, built one stretch at a time. Your line was let us rise up and build. What broken thing did you repair? Day seven hundred forty-three.

The wall is finished. And when the people gather inside it, it isn't for a parade. They gather in the open square by the Water Gate, men and women and everyone old enough to understand, and they ask Ezra the scribe to bring out the book of the law. Ezra climbs up onto a wooden platform built for the day, high enough that the whole crowd can see him. He opens the book, and the moment he opens it, the people stand. Then he reads, from early morning until midday, and everyone listens. Remember the lost book a few days ago, found in the temple and read first to a king? This time the people themselves ask for it. And then the crowd does something the leaders have to answer.

Before the reading, Ezra blesses the Lord, and the King James Bible says: "all the people answered, Amen, Amen, with lifting up their hands." Then the reading. And the leaders don't just read. Levites, the teachers, help the people understand: "they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading." Reading out loud, explaining, making sure people get it. And then the people understand, and it breaks them. "All the people wept, when they heard the words of the law." The text doesn't say why. Some readers hear grief at how far the people had wandered, like Josiah tearing his clothes. Here's where the story turns. Nehemiah and Ezra and the teachers stand up and stop the weeping. Not because grief is wrong, but because of what day it is. In the King James Bible: "Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength." Look at the order. Go eat something rich. Drink something sweet. And send some to the people who have nothing ready. Then the reason: the joy of the Lord is your strength. Notice whose joy it is: the joy of the Lord. In this chapter it isn't a mood anyone is told to manufacture. It holds people up, and it comes out as a shared meal. The chapter ends with the people going off to eat and drink and send portions, and to make great mirth, it says, "because they had understood the words that were declared unto them." Understanding led to tears first, then to a feast.

Here's the practice: plan a portion. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you've been heavy about lately, and let it be there. Then let your mind turn toward a table. What's something sweet or rich you could share today? A piece of cake, a coffee, fruit, a good meal. And who is someone for whom nothing is prepared: someone eating alone, someone new, someone who's had a hard week? Picture handing it to them. If you pray, you can thank God for the food before you share it. If you don't, just let the picture warm you. The bell holds the time.
Ezra. The scribe who read the law aloud until the people wept, then told them: go, eat, drink, and send portions to those with nothing ready, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.
Your line: joy is your strength. Today, share a treat with one person, and make sure it's someone for whom nothing is prepared. Day seven hundred forty-three.

744.title: Tobit and the angel
744.hook: in a book kept in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, young Tobias travels with a stranger who is Raphael
744.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians read Tobit as scripture, and Catholics honor Raphael as an archangel with a feast day; Tobit is sometimes read at Catholic weddings. Protestant churches don't count it as scripture, though some Protestants read it among the Apocrypha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ezra read to a weeping crowd that was told to go and feast. Your line was joy is your strength. Who did you share something sweet with? Day seven hundred forty-four.

A young man needs a guide for a long trip, so he goes out to find one, and the first person he meets is a friendly stranger who knows the road. They agree on a wage. The young man's mother cries as they leave. The family dog trots along behind them. That's the start of a journey in the book of Tobit, and it's worth knowing where to find it. Catholic and Orthodox Christians count Tobit among the books of the Bible. Protestant churches don't count it as scripture, and some Protestant Bibles print it in a separate section called the Apocrypha. So depending on whose Bible is on the shelf, it's either there or it isn't. The story inside it is today.

Tobit is an Israelite living in exile in Nineveh. He's the kind of man who gives to the poor and, at real risk, buries the bodies of his people left in the street. Then one night he sleeps outside by a wall, sparrow droppings fall into his eyes, and he goes blind. Worn out and humiliated, he prays to die. On the very same day, far away, a young woman named Sarah prays the same thing. She's been married seven times, the story says, and each husband was killed by a demon on the wedding night. Two people, two cities, two prayers of despair, and the book says both prayers were heard, and the angel Raphael was sent to heal them both. Tobit, thinking he's near the end, sends his son Tobias on a journey to collect money he once left in trust with a man named Gabael. Tobias needs a guide. The stranger he hires says his name is Azarias. Along the road a great fish leaps out of the river at Tobias, and the guide tells him to catch it and keep its heart, liver and gall. Those turn out to drive the demon away from Sarah, whom Tobias marries, and to heal Tobit's eyes when they get home. Only at the end, when the family tries to pay the guide, does he tell them who he is: Raphael, one of the seven holy angels who stand before God. He says he was there when Tobit prayed, and when he buried the dead. That's the turn worth carrying. The help didn't arrive with wings. It arrived as a hired traveling companion, walking the same dusty road, camping by the same river, and nobody knew until the trip was over.
screen: `A BLIND MAN AND A GRIEVING BRIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be good company on one road. Settle, and breathe. Think of a trip in the day ahead, however short: a walk to the shops, a school run, a bus ride, a drive to an appointment. Who could go with you, or whom could you go with? Someone nervous about where they're headed, someone who'd otherwise go alone. Picture the road. What would it mean to be a good companion on it: matching their pace, carrying a bag, listening more than talking, staying until they arrive? If you pray, you can bring that person and that road before God. If you don't, just walk it once in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Raphael. The hired guide on Tobias's long journey, who turns out to be the angel sent to heal blind Tobit and rescue Sarah.
Your line: an angel on the road. Today, travel kindly with someone, even a short trip, the way Raphael walked beside Tobias. Day seven hundred forty-four.

745.title: The Maccabees (1 Maccabees 4:36–59)
745.hook: after a desecration, the temple is cleansed and rededicated, the feast Jesus later attends
745.howItsDone: Jews keep Hanukkah for eight nights by lighting a menorah; Christians meet the feast in John 10:22, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians read 1 Maccabees as scripture, while some Protestants read it among the Apocrypha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raphael, a guide on the road nobody recognized. Your line was an angel on the road. Who did you travel kindly with? Day seven hundred forty-five.

"And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch." That's John's Gospel, chapter ten. It drops a festival into the story without explaining it. Which feast is that, and what was being dedicated? The answer is in a book written about a time when the temple had been taken from the people. A foreign king, Antiochus, had set an abomination on the altar and forced sacrifices the law forbade. A priest named Mattathias and his sons resisted, and in time his son Judas, called Maccabeus, led them. Today they've just won, and they walk up to the temple to see what's left.

First Maccabees is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, and some Protestant Bibles print it among the Apocrypha. Its account is vivid. Judas says to his brothers, in effect: our enemies are beaten, let us go up to cleanse and dedicate the sanctuary. They climb Mount Zion and find the sanctuary desolate, the altar profaned, the gates burned, and shrubs growing in the courts like a forest or a hillside. Their first response isn't to start scrubbing. They tear their clothes, put ashes on their heads, and fall on their faces. Grief comes first. Then the work. They choose priests who had kept the law. They take down the defiled altar, and here's a striking detail: they don't know what to do with its stones. So they store them on the temple mount until a prophet should come and tell them. They don't pretend to have an answer they don't have. They build a new altar of whole stones, make new holy vessels, light the lamps on the lampstand, and set out the bread. And early one morning they offer sacrifice on the new altar, with songs, harps and cymbals, and all the people fall on their faces and worship. Then Judas and the whole congregation decide that the days of the dedication of the altar should be kept every year, for eight days, with joy and gladness. That feast is Hanukkah, the Hebrew word for dedication, and Jewish tradition keeps it with lights for eight nights. Jewish tradition also tells a later story about a small jar of oil that lasted; 1 Maccabees itself doesn't tell that story. It tells of an altar rebuilt and a people giving the space back to God. And John's Gospel shows Jesus walking in that temple on that feast, in winter.

Here's the practice: rededicate one small space. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that was meant for good and got overgrown or misused: a room that's become a dumping ground, a morning hour lost to your phone, a friendship gone sour, a habit that used to be prayer and is now just noise. Like the Maccabees, let yourself be sad about it first. Then choose the one thing you'd clear and give back. If you pray, you can give it back to God in your own words. If you don't, just name what it's for again. The bell holds the time.
Hanukkah. Dedication: the feast that remembers the temple cleansed and its altar rededicated, kept for eight days, and the feast of the dedication John's Gospel names.
Your line: rededicate. Today, light one light, a candle or a lamp, and if you like, do it again each night for eight nights as you clear that one space. Day seven hundred forty-five.

746.title: Between the testaments
746.hook: the quieter centuries: Greek rule, then Rome, synagogues everywhere, and people waiting
746.howItsDone: Some Christians meet the years between the testaments through the people waiting at the start of the Gospels, like Simeon and Anna, and churches that keep Advent take up that same waiting in the weeks before Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Maccabees cleansed the temple, and Hanukkah remembers it. Your line was rededicate. What small space did you clear and give back? Day seven hundred forty-six.

Open a King James Bible printed without the Apocrypha, turn to the last page of the Old Testament, and you land in Malachi. Its final verses look forward: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD." Then you turn one page, and you're in Matthew, with a family tree and a baby. In your hands it's one page. In history it's a long stretch of time, the gap between the two testaments. Some readers call them the silent years. But they weren't silent. They were waiting years, and today is about what the waiting looked like.

Here is that stretch in a few strokes. First Maccabees opens with Alexander the Great sweeping through, and with the Greek kings who came after him ruling the land, and yesterday's story, the Maccabees and the rededicated temple, happens in those years. Then Rome arrives. By the time the Gospels open, Luke's account of the birth opens with a Roman emperor: "there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed." Meanwhile something quieter grows: the synagogue, a gathering for reading and prayer. In Acts, James puts it this way: "Moses of old time hath in every city them that preach him, being read in the synagogues every sabbath day." When Jesus appears in Nazareth, Luke says "as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day." A custom. Something that had been going on long enough to become habit. And through it all, people wait. Luke gives two of them names. Simeon, a man in Jerusalem, "just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel." And Anna, a prophet who never left the temple, who spoke of the child "to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem." Waiting, in these pages, isn't doing nothing. It's showing up, reading, praying, keeping the customs, for years, without seeing the thing you're waiting for. Paul, writing later as a follower of Jesus, looks back on it this way: "when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son." Some readers hear in that word something filling slowly. And this closes a long run: from Joshua at the Jordan, through judges and kings, Ruth and Samuel, David and Solomon, Elijah and Elisha, the fall and the exile, Esther, Ezra and Nehemiah, all the way to people standing in the temple, waiting.

Here's the practice: wait with hope for two minutes. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you're waiting for: news, healing, a reconciliation, a change in the world, a change in yourself. Don't try to hurry it. Don't give up on it either. Just hold it the way Simeon might have, showing up one more day. Notice what waiting feels like in your body, and let your breath slow down around it. If you pray, you can bring that waiting to God. If you don't, just keep it company. The bell holds the time.
Simeon. A man in Jerusalem waiting for the consolation of Israel, one face of the long stretch between Malachi and Matthew, through Greek rule, then Rome, and synagogues.

Your line: the waiting years. That closes this part of the path, Joshua to the return. Tomorrow the long story turns to the early church. Today, keep one small custom while you wait for something. Day seven hundred forty-six.

747.title: What happened to the twelve
747.hook: church traditions send Thomas to India, Andrew to Greece, James to Spain; tradition says many died as martyrs
747.howItsDone: Churches remember the apostles on their feast days, and churches in India, Greece, Spain and elsewhere keep the traditions of the apostles linked to them. Churches also pray, in their services, for Christians who face persecution.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon, and your line was the waiting years. What were you waiting on? Today the long story turns a page, into the early church. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

Near the end of Mark's Gospel, the King James Bible gives the whole mission of the eleven in one line: "And they went forth, and preached every where." It's a short sentence for a very long road. After it, the New Testament mostly follows Peter and Paul, and the rest of the twelve slip quietly out of the story. Andrew, who went and found his brother Simon. Thomas, who said he wouldn't believe until he saw the wounds. Bartholomew, Matthew, Thaddaeus, Simon the Canaanite. The Bible doesn't say where they went. But the churches didn't forget them. Some churches still tell, with real pride, which apostle brought them the faith. Today's word is how those stories traveled.

The word is tradition: something handed on, from one person to the next. Paul uses it plainly: "hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle." Not only letters. Word of mouth, too. And the stories of where the twelve went came down mostly that way. Here is what church tradition says. Thomas, the one who doubted, went east, as far as India, and Christians in Kerala, in the south of India, call themselves Saint Thomas Christians and trace their church to him. Andrew went to Greece, and Greek tradition remembers his death at Patras. James, the brother of John, is linked by Spanish tradition to Santiago de Compostela, where pilgrims still walk the long road to his shrine. And tradition says that many of the twelve died as martyrs. Now the honest part. These are traditions, not chapters of the Bible. Some are old, some grew later, and historians weigh each one on its own. Apart from Judas, Acts tells the death of just one of the twelve, and it's short and hard: Herod "killed James the brother of John with the sword." That's the same James, and the Spanish tradition holds that his body was carried to Spain afterward. Catholic and Orthodox teaching gives tradition real weight alongside scripture; Protestant churches teach that every tradition is tested by scripture. But all of them can hear what these stories are doing. In Acts, before he is taken up, Jesus says: "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth." The traditions are a map of people taking that sentence seriously. And some of the places on that map are still places where being a Christian costs something.
screen: `TO THE UTTERMOST PART OF THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep someone far away company. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind Christians somewhere in the world who gather quietly because gathering openly isn't safe, or whose church has been burned, or who are watched. You don't need names or a map. Just let them be real: a few people, a borrowed room, a door shut before the reading starts. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words, or simply hold them before God. If you don't pray, hold them in your attention, the way you'd think of a friend who's far away and having a hard time. The bell holds the time.
Tradition. Something handed on, by letter or by word of mouth. Here, the stories of where the twelve went, kept by the churches that remember them.
Your line: they went everywhere. Today, learn the name of one place where Christians face danger for their faith, and carry it with you for the day. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

748.title: The council of Jerusalem (Acts 15)
748.hook: a great argument: must Gentiles become Jews? they decide not to trouble them
748.carry: it seemed good to the spirit and us
748.howItsDone: Churches have looked to Acts 15 as a pattern for settling disagreements: meeting together, hearing what people have seen, reading scripture, and seeking the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word was tradition, and your line was they went everywhere. Which place did you carry with you? Today, before anyone goes much further, there's an argument to settle. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

Antioch, a big city in Syria, and a growing church where Gentiles, people who aren't Jewish, have been joining. Then visitors arrive from Judaea with a hard message. In the King James Bible they say: "Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved." The letter later says these visitors "went out from us," from the church in Jerusalem. Their question is honest: if Gentiles are joining the people of Israel's God, shouldn't they keep Israel's covenant? Paul and Barnabas disagree, loudly. The text calls it "no small dissension and disputation." Nobody can settle it in Antioch. So the church sends Paul, Barnabas and some others up to Jerusalem.

Acts fifteen is a meeting, and it reads like one. "And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter." There's much disputing. Then Peter stands up and tells what he saw: God giving the Holy Spirit to Gentiles, with no difference made. He ends: "we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they." Notice the direction of that. Not they'll be saved like us. We, like them. Then the room goes quiet and listens to Barnabas and Paul tell what they saw among the Gentiles. Then James, whom Paul elsewhere calls "James the Lord's brother," sums it up: "my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God." Don't trouble them. Instead they send a short letter asking a few things: keep away from food offered to idols, from blood, from what's strangled, from sexual immorality. Some readers hear in that list the old rules for strangers living among Israel. And the letter has the line that gives us today's carry: "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things." Look at that sentence. The Holy Spirit, and us. Not one without the other. The decision came out of argument, testimony, scripture and listening, and they still spoke as people trying to follow God rather than win. Some churches still turn to this chapter when they disagree. When the letter is read in Antioch, the text says, "they rejoiced for the consolation." A fight, settled, and the people who received it were glad.

Here's the practice: settle a quarrel without extra weight. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one disagreement that's still open: at home, at work, in a club, in a church. Notice what you've been asking of the other side. All of it. Now ask the council's question: what's actually necessary here? What could you set down, and let them keep their way? You don't have to settle it in two minutes. Just find the one burden you could take off. If you pray, you can bring the quarrel to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
James. The Lord's brother, whose sentence at the Jerusalem council was not to trouble Gentile believers with more than the necessary things.
Your line: it seemed good to the spirit and us. Today, in one decision you share with someone, ask what's necessary, and drop one thing that isn't. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

749.title: Paul's journeys
749.hook: many miles on foot and by sea, making tents to pay his way
749.howItsDone: Christians read Paul's journeys in Acts and in his letters, often with the maps printed in the back of some Bibles, and people who serve a church while working an ordinary job are sometimes called tentmakers after him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, James, and your line was it seemed good to the spirit and us. What did you set down that wasn't necessary? Now the road is open. Day seven hundred forty-nine.
screen: `IT SEEMED GOOD TO THE SPIRIT AND US.`

segments.voice: A workshop in Corinth. Needles, heavy thread, a length of rough material pinned across a bench, and three people working it: a married couple, Aquila and Priscilla, and a traveler who has just arrived from Athens. Acts says it simply: "because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers." The traveler is Paul. His road fills the later chapters of Acts. And on a weekday in Corinth he is sewing tents to pay his way. Today is about the roads he walked, and the work he did with his hands along the way.

Acts follows Paul out of Antioch, with Barnabas, across the sea to Cyprus and up into the hill towns of Asia Minor. Later, in Troas on the coast, he sees a man in the night, in a vision, saying: "Come over into Macedonia, and help us." So he crosses into Europe. In Philippi a businesswoman named Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, opens her home to the new church. Then Thessalonica, Berea, Athens, Corinth, Ephesus. Acts never numbers his trips. Readers draw them as journeys on maps in the back of their Bibles, but Acts tells it as one long road. And the road was hard. Paul lists it himself, in a letter to Corinth: "Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep; In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers." Then, the tents. Why work at all? Paul tells the Thessalonians: "labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you." He didn't want the message to come with a bill. To the elders of Ephesus he holds up his own hands: "these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me." Not only his own needs. His friends' too. So the picture of Paul isn't just the preacher in the marketplace. It's the man at the bench with a needle in his hand, who also "reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath." Some Christians who work ordinary jobs while serving a church call themselves tentmakers, after him.

Here's the practice: walk Paul's road on a map. If you have a phone or an atlas handy, find the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea. Look for Antioch in the corner where Turkey meets Syria, then Cyprus, then Philippi in northern Greece, then Athens and Corinth to the south, then Ephesus across the water. Trace the line slowly with a finger. If you can't look at a map right now, close your eyes and walk it in your mind: a coast, a ship, a dusty road, a workshop. If you pray, you can pray for someone traveling today. The bell holds the time.
Paul's journeys. The roads and sea crossings Acts follows, from Antioch to Europe and back, paid for by a tentmaker's hands.
